title: Everything is information
summary: Encode text as bits and see how a machine decodes a message.

scenario.briefing: The robotics lab only accepts bytes. Send the two-letter message HI using the reference table. One wrong bit changes the command.

objectives.description: Explain why bit positions have different values.
Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Each character uses eight bits. Start with H.
Read the reference table row for H, then the row for I.
The first byte is 01001000 and the second is 01001001.
Set the first byte to 01001000 and the second to 01001001.

misconceptions.description: Reading bits in the wrong order.
misconceptions.feedback: The table reads left to right from the most significant bit. Reversing each byte changes every character.

misconceptions.description: Treating a decimal digit as one bit.
misconceptions.feedback: A byte has eight bits. The decimal number 8 is not the same as one bit.

sections.title: Bits are a choice of two states
sections.body: A bit stores one of two values, often written 0 and 1. A group of eight bits is a byte and can represent 256 different patterns. Text, images, and instructions are all encoded as patterns with agreed meanings.

sections.title: Encoding needs an agreement
sections.body: The pattern 01001000 means H only because both sides agree on an encoding such as ASCII. A different encoding could assign a different character. Data without context is just bits.

vocabulary.definition: A value with exactly two possible states.
Eight bits treated as one unit.
An agreed mapping between symbols and patterns.

steps.title: Encode the control message
steps.prompt: Set every bit so the two bytes encode the message HI. Use the reference table.
steps.explanation: H is 01001000 and I is 01001001 in ASCII. The lab receives two complete bytes.

steps.title: What do the bits mean?
steps.prompt: Select every accurate statement about bits and encoding.

statements.label: A bit can represent exactly two states.
Bits need an encoding agreement to become text.
The decimal digit 8 is the same thing as one bit.
A byte always represents one letter.

steps.explanation: Bits hold two states. A byte can encode a letter under an agreement, but it can also hold a number, part of an image, or a machine instruction.

steps.title: Why eight bits?
steps.prompt: Eight bits can form 256 distinct patterns. Why does that matter for encoding?

options.label: It gives enough distinct patterns for many common characters and control codes.
It makes every message exactly eight times faster.
It matches the decimal number 256 exactly.
The number eight has no special meaning.

quiz.explanation: A larger set of patterns can represent more symbols. 256 is enough for ASCII and many control codes, though not every writing system.

hints: Count the possible patterns from eight bits: two choices each.
More patterns means more possible symbols.
256 different patterns is enough for a common character set.
The number of distinct patterns determines how many symbols the encoding can cover.

accessibility.summary: Each bit is a checkbox with a visible 0 or 1 label. The reference table is real table markup.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Tab through the bit toggles and press Space to change a bit.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each toggle announces its character, byte, bit position, and current value. The encoded bytes are read as digits.
